name: Customer support
title: AI prompts for customer support replies
seoTitle: Customer Service Prompts: 6 AI Reply Templates
description: Free AI prompt templates for customer support: calm replies to angry customers, refusing refunds, FAQ answers, triage and macros that never overpromise.
intro: In support, the dangerous AI failure isn't a bad tone — it is a promise your policy does not allow. Each template pastes your policy in and forbids commitments outside it.

templates.title: Reply to an angry customer
templates.useWhen: A customer is upset and the reply must calm things down.
templates.prompt:
Write a reply to the customer message between <<< and >>>.
Our policy on this: <<<[PASTE THE RELEVANT POLICY]>>>
What we can actually offer: [OPTIONS]
Rules: the first sentence acknowledges the specific problem (not “sorry for any inconvenience”); explain what happens next, with a time frame only if the policy gives one; never promise refunds, credits or dates beyond the policy; under 120 words; no blame on the customer.

Message: <<<[PASTE]>>>
templates.why: Specific acknowledgement de-escalates; pasting the policy bounds what the reply can promise.

templates.title: Say no to a refund politely
templates.useWhen: The answer is no and it has to stay polite.
templates.prompt:
A customer asked for a refund we can't give because [REASON]. Policy: <<<[PASTE POLICY LINE]>>>
Write a reply that states the decision clearly in the first two sentences, explains the reason in plain words citing the policy, offers [ALTERNATIVE, if any] and leaves a door open ([HOW TO ESCALATE]). Warm, but no apology for the policy itself. Under 130 words.
templates.why: A vague “no” generates a second email. A clear decision, the reason and an alternative close the loop.

templates.title: Turn a policy into a FAQ answer
templates.useWhen: Customers keep asking the same question.
templates.prompt:
Turn this internal policy into a customer-facing FAQ answer: <<<[PASTE POLICY]>>>
Format: the question as a customer would type it; a one-sentence direct answer; then up to 4 bullets with conditions or exceptions. Plain language, no internal jargon. Don't add anything the policy doesn't say — if something customers will ask is unclear in the policy, list it for me separately.
templates.why: A direct answer first matches how people scan FAQs, and the list of unclear points improves the policy, not just the copy.

templates.title: Triage incoming messages
templates.useWhen: The inbox is full and you need to know what to answer first.
templates.prompt:
Classify each message below into one of these categories: [CATEGORIES, e.g. billing, bug, how-to, cancellation, other].
For each message: category, urgency (high = [YOUR DEFINITION]), a one-line summary, and whether it needs a human.
If a message fits no category, or two, say so — don't force it.

Messages: <<<[PASTE, one per line with an ID]>>>
templates.why: Defined categories and a definition of “high urgency” keep classification consistent; allowing “doesn't fit” exposes gaps in your categories.

templates.title: Write a reusable support macro
templates.useWhen: The same situation comes up every week.
templates.prompt:
Write a reusable reply template for [SITUATION, e.g. delayed delivery].
Fixed parts: our policy <<<[PASTE]>>> and our tone ([2–3 WORDS]).
Leave named slots for the variable parts: [CUSTOMER NAME], [ORDER NUMBER], [NEW DATE] and so on.
Add a checklist of 3 things the agent must verify before sending.
templates.why: Macros speed support up but go wrong when sent unchecked. Named slots plus a pre-send checklist keep both speed and accuracy.

templates.title: Turn a complaint into a bug report
templates.useWhen: A customer describes a problem the product team must fix.
templates.prompt:
Turn this customer message into a bug report for our developers: <<<[PASTE]>>>
Format: title; steps to reproduce (only what the customer actually said — mark unknowns as “unknown”); expected vs actual behaviour; device or browser if mentioned; a severity guess with the reason.
Also write 2 questions to ask the customer to fill in the unknowns.
templates.why: Developers need reproducible steps. Marking unknowns instead of guessing prevents wild-goose chases.
